title: Icons and illustration as part of the system
metaTitle: Icon system design: stroke, grid, subject
excerpt: Pick one stroke, one grid, and a limit on what icons may depict. Mixing three downloaded styles makes a product look assembled rather than designed.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. The drawing is a set of marks with one job, the way an icon family should be.
caption: One family of marks, drawn to a grid. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a small icon system?
faqs.answer: Choose a stroke, a grid, and the kind of subject the icons may depict. Store them under names that say the action, shared by the design file and the code. Leave illustration for empty states and marketing moments, at a larger size.

faqs.question: Can a product mix icon packs?
faqs.answer: Mixing a thin outline set, a filled set, and a hand-drawn set makes the interface look assembled from downloads. Keep the family that already covers most of the product, and redraw the strangers on the same grid. Delete unused files so the next person does not import them.

faqs.question: Do icons need text names?
faqs.answer: An icon that is the only label on a button needs a text name in the markup, so the control can be understood and operated. A decorative icon beside a visible word should not be announced a second time. Treat that rule as part of the system, alongside stroke and grid.

markdown:
Icon system design starts with three choices: a stroke, a grid, and the kind of thing the icons are allowed to depict. Make those choices once, and every new symbol has somewhere to land. Mix a thin outline set, a filled set, and a hand-drawn set, and the product looks assembled from downloads.

The system is small on purpose. A young product needs a few dozen symbols that behave like one family. It does not need a library that covers every metaphor in the world.

## Stroke, grid, and subject

Pick the stroke before you draw the second icon. A 1.5 pixel stroke at the size you actually use, with rounded or square caps, and the same corner treatment on every shape. If some icons are filled and some are stroked, decide which jobs get which treatment. Navigation can be stroked. A status that must read at a glance can be filled. Switching treatment because a particular metaphor was easier to find in another pack is how the family breaks.

The grid is the frame each icon is drawn in. A 24 pixel grid with a live area inset from the edge keeps optical sizes even. A 16 pixel grid is a different decision for dense product UI. Draw both only if you truly ship both sizes, and draw the smaller one on purpose. Shrinking a 24 pixel icon and hoping the strokes survive is how hairlines disappear.

Subject matter is the decision teams skip. Choose what the icons show. Objects and simple actions, such as a document, a search mark, a warning. Refuse metaphors that require a caption to be guessed, and refuse illustration that belongs in the empty state instead. An icon of a person, a gear, and a house can coexist. An icon of a person, a watercolor bird, and a glossy 3D cube cannot, because they are three different products.

## One family, named files

Store the icons as a named set, in the design file and in the repository. The name should say the action or the object, not the picture. `search` is a name. `magnifying-glass-outline-final-2` is a download. The same name in Figma and in code means an engineer can add the symbol the design already uses.

Hanabi builds product interfaces in React and TypeScript, so an icon is a small component that inherits the text color around it. Current color is the right default. An icon with its own baked-in hex value will ignore the theme and sit in the wrong color beside a label. If a status icon needs a fixed color, that color is a token, shared with the text that states the same status.

Keep the set in one folder. A second folder of "temporary" icons becomes the real set by the third sprint. If a screen needs a symbol you do not have, draw it on the grid or choose a different label. Importing one icon from a second library, even a good library, imports a second stroke.

## Where icons stop and illustration starts

Icons are for recognition inside the interface: navigation, actions, and status. Illustration is for a moment that needs tone: an empty screen, an error that should feel calm, a section of the marketing site. They can share a visual idea, such as the same line weight or the same limited palette, and they should not be used as substitutes for each other.

A row of navigation items made of small illustrations will be slow to scan and inconsistent the moment someone adds a new item. A full-bleed empty state made of a 16 pixel icon will look unfinished. Write the rule down in a sentence the next person can follow. Icons at interface size. Illustration at the sizes you listed. Nothing in between unless you add it to the system on purpose.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treat web content as something people have to perceive and operate, and the guidelines apply to text, images, and the markup around them. An icon that is the only label on a button needs a text name in that markup. A decorative icon next to a visible word should not be announced twice. Those are system rules, the same as stroke and grid. A downloaded SVG that ships with a random title, or with no name at all, fails them by accident.

## What to do with the set you already have

Most early products do not have a clean start. They have a navigation bar from one set, a settings page from another, and a marketing section from a third. Fix it by inventory, not by buying a larger pack.

List every icon on the site and in the product. Group them by stroke and by style. You will usually find one family that already covers most of the interface, and a handful of strangers. Keep the family. Redraw the strangers on the same grid, or replace them with a label until there is time to redraw. Delete the unused files so nobody imports them next month.

While you redraw, check the optical size. A circle and a square at the same pixel dimensions do not look the same size. Adjust the live area so the symbols feel even in a row. This is the kind of care that makes a small set look intentional. A large set with uneven sizes looks cheaper.

Document the don'ts beside the grid. No mixing fills and strokes inside one toolbar. No dropping a brand logo into the icon size and calling it an icon. No stretching to fill a wide button. A picture of the happy set, without those lines, will be ignored the first time someone is in a hurry.

## Photography is a different decision

Icons and illustration are drawn. Photography is chosen. A brand that is calm in photographs and noisy in icons has not finished the system. Direction for pictures covers subject, crop, and what you will not show. That is the next decision if the drawn set is now under control: [photography and illustration direction for a young brand](/blog/photography-and-illustration-direction).

The two should be able to sit on the same page without one apologizing for the other. If they cannot, the page is telling you the system is still two moods.

If you want the interface symbols drawn as part of the product, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). A small icon family is part of the build, not a pack added the week before launch.
